keyPoints.line: or measure: the spec says which.

read.where: **Simple syrup** is **1:1** sugar to water; **rich** is **2:1**. Difford’s Guide notes that measuring by **weight** gives a sweeter syrup than measuring by **volume**, so the recipe has to say which. Make it the same way every batch, or every drink changes.
read.mixup: A cup of sugar doesn’t weigh the same as a cup of water. That’s why weight and volume give different syrups.
read.sayIt: We make our syrups here, the same way every batch.

stops.name: Weight or volume
stops.text: The **recipe** says which. Weight gives a sweeter syrup.

keyPoints.line: is thinned so it mixes into a cold drink.
every syrup gets one, written down.

read.where: **Honey** straight from the jar seizes up in a cold drink, so it’s thinned with water into **honey syrup** (our Gold Rush and Bee’s Knees). **Demerara** syrup brings a caramel note. Ginger, spice or herb syrups bring theirs. Our **Penicillin** uses **honey-ginger syrup**. Every house syrup gets a **written recipe**, so any shift can make it.
read.mixup: Honey syrup and honey aren’t the same amount in a spec. Use the syrup the spec names.
read.sayIt: It’s sweetened with a honey-ginger syrup we make here.

stops.name: Honey syrup
stops.text: Honey **thinned** so it mixes: Gold Rush, Bee’s Knees.

keyPoints.line: with little white pith; pith is bitter.
lets the sugar draw out the oil.

read.bigIdea: Sugar pulls the oil out of citrus peel.
read.where: **Oleo saccharum** is a syrup made from **citrus peel and sugar**. Sugar draws water and the fragrant **oils** out of the peel. Peel the fruit with as little **white pith** as you can (pith is bitter), toss the peels with sugar, let it sit, then **strain**. It’s the base of classic **punch**. Difford’s Guide also describes a faster vacuum-bag method.
read.mixup: Oleo isn’t juice. It’s the peel’s oil; use the peeled fruit for juice.
read.sayIt: It’s sweetened with an oleo: sugar that’s pulled the oils out of citrus peel.

stops.name: Sugar
stops.text: Toss the peels with **sugar** and let it sit.

keyPoints.line: often: chili and tea go fast.
infuse a fat, chill, strain it out.
what’s in it, and the date.

read.bigIdea: Steep a flavor into the spirit.
read.where: An **infusion** steeps fruit, spice, tea or chili in a spirit, then strains it out. Strong flavors (**chili**, **tea**) can take minutes or hours, so **taste often**. **Fat-washing** infuses a fat, like bacon fat or butter, then chills it so the fat sets and **strains** it out; Difford’s credits PDT’s bacon Old Fashioned with making it popular. Label every bottle with **what’s in it** (allergens too) and the **date**.
read.mixup: A fat-washed spirit still carries that food. Butter-washed means dairy: tell the guest, and put it in the Allergen Guide.
read.sayIt: It’s washed with brown butter, so it has dairy in it. Is that okay for you?
